claims.text: Eutectic high-entropy alloys have dual-phase lamellar colonies containing numerous internal boundaries.
Internal boundaries in the lamellar colonies act as crack-initiation sites during room-temperature tensile deformation.
A small addition of a boundary-active dopant will segregate to lamellar interfaces.
Dopant segregation will enhance cohesion at the lamellar interfaces.
Boundary-segregated dopant atoms will reduce local stress concentrations.
Boundary-segregated dopant atoms will mitigate microcrack initiation.
Enhanced interfacial cohesion will improve load transfer along lamellar interfaces during tensile loading.
Improved load transfer and suppressed microcrack initiation will simultaneously increase tensile strength and room-temperature ductility.
The doped alloy will show statistically significant increases in both tensile strength and elongation to failure relative to the undoped baseline.
The undoped baseline has coarse interfacial bonding that leads to premature microcrack formation and limited tensile ductility.
The beneficial effect exists only within a narrow dopant-concentration window.
Formation of deleterious brittle secondary phases will prevent the proposed benefit.
The proposed improvement is specific to alloy systems with dual-phase lamellar microstructures.
Variability in dopant segregation behavior may affect reproducibility.

contradictions.description: The experiment calls the doped and undoped samples 'identical compositions,' although adding a dopant necessarily changes composition. They could instead share the same nominal base composition apart from the dopant addition.
